newsitem.title: GUATEMALA: In a year, Arzu steers Guatemala to peace.
newsitem.headline: In a year, Arzu steers Guatemala to peace.

text.p: President Alvaro Arzu, who on Sunday was due to sign a peace treaty with leftist rebels, has stunned the region with the speed in which he ended a war that for 36 years darkened the country with shame.
Less than a year after taking office, the 50-year-old former businessman is basking in high acclaim accross Latin America for his efforts to heal a nation torn by fratricide.

A blond, blue-eyed member of Guatemala's white elite, who can trace his ancestry back to 17th century Russia, Arzu was shrugged off by many as a bland tool of the private sector when he came to power last January.
But pragmatically, he sensed that the two arch-foes in the conflict, the army and the Guatemalan National Revolutionary Unit (URNG) rebels, were ready to bury the hatchet.

"Even before he took office he met with the URNG and made very clear to them his commitment to achieve peace," the government's chief negotiator Gustavo Porras told Reuters. "He left them with no doubt that he does what he says."
With a businessman's brain, Arzu has pursued peace, aware that Guatemala must shed its image of conflict and human rights abuse to attract investment and join the global economy.
He also earned plaudits for an agreement to shrink the 43,000-strong army by a third, and for a bold and unprecedented purge this year of corrupt military officials.
His ability to rein in the army, that has for decades lorded over Guatemala like a mediaeval fiefdom, is considered his main achievement in a year he describes as an "eternity".

In a country once considered to have the worst human rights record in Latin America, where 140,000 people died or "disappeared" in army counterinsurgency sweeps, Arzu says he is surprised at how readily the military succumbed to peace.
But he has also offered them escape from potentially devastating humiliations by including an amnesty in the peace treaty that will cover all but the most brutal war crimes.
"Who in Guatemala can cast the first stone?" he told Reuters on Friday, broadly admitting that most sectors of the blood-stained country have guilty pasts that make reconciliation possible.
He played down his own role in the peace process, thanking God instead. But analysts say there is little doubt his iron will helped steer the warring factions to a peace settlement.

Indeed, the former boxer and squash champion hits out angrily when critics challenge the sturdiness of a peace accord that relies on billions of dollars of as yet undelivered foreign aid, and is considered by some on the left as a sell-out by the URNG.
At a recent news conference, he blasted human rights groups and even the local press for challenging the peace accords.

"He has a very strong character and a determination that things should progress. For that people have to regain confidence," Porras said. "What most affects him is pessimism. He's very sensitive to that."
The reluctance to accept criticism, his opponents say, may cost him support next year as he faces the far more difficult job of satisfying expectations raised by peace.
"This is an intolerant, authoritarian, overbearing government. It doesn't listen. We need someone tolerant," former government peace negotiator Hector Rosada said.
